strengths: The paper provides a clear theoretical motivation for the method: Theorem 3.2 formally shows that block-level joint modeling strictly reduces the achievable NELBO relative to token-wise independence, extending prior single-token results (Liu et al. 2025a; Kang et al. 2026) to arbitrary block sizes B>1 with an explicit expression for the gap.

Theorem 3.3 gives a compelling theoretical justification for the specific design choice of soft-conditioning (feeding full marginals rather than hard top-k tokens) to the auxiliary AR model, including a concrete counter-example showing that top-k truncation can exclude the true joint mode. This is directly validated empirically in the soft-vs-hard ablation (Table 1), where switching to top-1 conditioning causes a large accuracy drop, providing good internal consistency between theory and experiment.

The proposed architecture is practical and lightweight: it freezes the large DLM backbone and only finetunes a small (0.6B) auxiliary AR model, which is an efficient and reproducible design compared to alternatives (e.g., ADJUST) that require training an auxiliary model from scratch.

Empirical results show a consistent Pareto improvement (Pass@1 vs. throughput) over both the base Dream-Coder-Instruct-7B model and the ADJUST baseline across six code-generation benchmarks (HumanEval/+, MBPP/+, BigCodeBench full/hard), for both static and dynamic parallelism regimes.
The appendix provides substantial implementation detail (training hyperparameters, tokenizer alignment handling, decoding mechanism, hardware) that supports reproducibility.
The paper is transparent about design limitations, e.g., explicitly reporting the accuracy/throughput trade-off of the candidate-scoping heuristic (Table 2) rather than hiding it.
weaknesses: Evaluation is restricted to a single base DLM (Dream-Coder-Instruct-7B) and a single domain (Python code generation); no experiments on general natural-language generation or other DLM backbones are provided, which limits confidence that the claimed 'new Pareto frontier' generalizes beyond this narrow setting.

All reported results appear to be single-run (n=1, fixed seed) with no variance/confidence intervals, which is a concern given that HumanEval has only 164 problems and Pass@1 differences between methods can be small at some throughput levels.

Only one prior coherence-enhancing baseline (ADJUST) is empirically compared, despite the related-work section discussing many other relevant methods (APD, FlashDLLM, TiDAR, discrete copula diffusion); while some architectural differences make head-to-head comparison harder, the lack of any quantitative comparison to these methods weakens the significance claims.

Throughput results are reported only at batch size 1; there is no analysis of how the two-model (DLM + AR) architecture scales under batched inference, which is important for assessing real-world deployment value of the claimed speedups.

The 'candidate scoping' heuristic that restricts unmasking to the nearest 10 blocks is somewhat ad hoc, is acknowledged to trade off accuracy for stability, and its interaction with the theoretical claims (e.g., full block independence) is not analyzed formally.

There is no scaling study of the auxiliary AR model size (only Qwen3-0.6B is used); it is unclear how sensitive the method is to AR capacity, or whether even smaller/larger AR models would change the accuracy-throughput trade-off substantially.

The theoretical contribution, while a useful generalization, builds incrementally on existing total-correlation/NELBO decomposition results (as the authors themselves note), so its novelty is more in the extension to blocks than a fundamentally new theoretical insight.

strengths: The paper is built on a clear theoretical motivation: Theorem 3.2 formalizes how block-wise conditional independence strictly reduces the irreducible NELBO relative to token-wise independence, and Theorem 3.3 gives a principled Fréchet-class argument for why soft (full-marginal) conditioning is necessary rather than top-k/top-1 truncated signals -- this nicely explains why prior top-1-conditioned verifier approaches (e.g., APD, FlashDLLM) may be fundamentally limited.

The soft-conditioning ablation (Table 1) directly supports the theoretical claim, showing a large accuracy drop when switching from soft (marginal) to hard (top-1) conditioning, which is a useful validation of the core design choice.

The empirical Pareto frontier plots (Figure 4) show consistent improvement over both the vanilla Dream-Coder static-parallel baseline and the ADJUST baseline across six coding benchmarks, suggesting the method has some practical value in the static-parallelism regime.

The idea of delegating local coherence to a tiny pretrained AR model (0.6B) that only ever attends to a short block (rather than the whole sequence) is a reasonable and relatively cheap way to inject local joint-modeling capacity without retraining the large DLM backbone, and is clearly differentiated from prior left-to-right/global-verifier approaches in the related work discussion.
weaknesses: All experiments use a single base DLM (Dream-Coder-Instruct-7B) and a single domain (Python code generation); there is no evidence the approach generalizes to natural language, other DLM backbones, or other AR auxiliary model families, despite the paper's general framing ('Diffusion Language Models', not just code models).

All results are produced on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU with n=1 sampling and a single fixed seed (explicitly stated in Appendix A.2); no variance, confidence intervals, or multiple-seed results are reported, making it hard to assess whether the reported Pass@1 gains (sometimes a few points) are statistically meaningful, especially on small benchmarks like HumanEval (164 problems).

Latency/throughput is only measured at batch size 1; this is a weak proxy for realistic deployment where batched generation and KV-cache reuse dominate practical speed considerations, and the paper does not address how the two-model (DLM+AR) pipeline would behave under batching or memory pressure at scale.

The auxiliary AR model must be separately fine-tuned for each block size (B=2,4,8), which triples training cost and deployment complexity; no analysis is given of whether a single AR model could generalize across block sizes, undermining the 'lightweight/compact' framing when multiplied by the number of configurations needed in practice.

The 'candidate scoping' trick (restricting unmasking to the nearest 10 blocks to avoid premature EOS) is an ad hoc patch rather than a principled solution, and the paper admits the underlying EOS-prediction instability is unresolved, raising concerns about the robustness of the dynamic parallelism results.

Coherence improvements are only evaluated indirectly via downstream Pass@1; there is no direct quantitative measure of local coherence (e.g., perplexity under a strong reference model, human/LLM-judged fluency, or a targeted coherence probing benchmark), so attributing accuracy gains specifically to 'coherence' rather than general model capacity/regularization effects from the auxiliary AR model is not fully substantiated.

Comparisons are limited to only one directly competing method (ADJUST); several other related approaches discussed in Section 5 (APD, FlashDLLM, discrete copula diffusion, TiDAR, self-speculative masked diffusion) are not empirically compared against, despite being conceptually close alternatives, limiting the strength of the claimed 'new Pareto frontier.'

Absolute accuracy on harder benchmarks (e.g., BigCodeBench-hard, <20% Pass@1 across all methods) remains low, raising questions about the practical significance of the reported improvements in realistic coding-assistant settings.

The theoretical contribution (Theorem 3.2) is explicitly described as an incremental generalization of prior block-independence results (Huang et al. 2022; Liu et al. 2025a; Kang et al. 2026; Zhong et al. 2026) to B>1, somewhat limiting the originality claimed for the theoretical component; the main novelty rests on the soft-conditioning interface engineering, which, while reasonable, is a comparatively modest technical contribution.

strengths: Clean theoretical grounding: Theorem 3.2 formally generalizes prior block-independence NELBO analyses to arbitrary block size B and explicitly quantifies the gap B1 - BB via total correlation, providing a principled motivation for block-wise rather than token-wise modeling.

Theorem 3.3 gives a compelling information-theoretic argument (via the Fréchet class / copula perspective) for why soft-conditioning (full marginals) is necessary and sufficient, whereas hard/top-k conditioning used by competing methods (e.g., APD, FlashDLLM) can provably exclude the true global mode -- a nice theoretical differentiator from prior left-to-right verification approaches.

The soft-conditioning mechanism is a practical and lightweight solution to the intractability of modeling the full joint over V^B, re-using a small pretrained AR model (Qwen3-0.6B) with minimal finetuning rather than training an auxiliary model from scratch (as ADJUST does).

Strong empirical validation: CoDiLA establishes a new Pareto frontier (accuracy vs. throughput) across six code benchmarks (HumanEval(+), MBPP(+), BigCodeBench full/hard) against both the base DLM and the closest competitor (ADJUST), with both static and dynamic parallelism regimes evaluated.
The soft-vs-hard conditioning ablation (Table 1) directly and convincingly supports the central theoretical claim (Theorem 3.3), showing large accuracy drops when truncating to top-1 conditioning.
Reasonably thorough reproducibility: detailed appendix with training hyperparameters, tokenizer alignment details, decoding procedure, and hardware/environment specification.
weaknesses: All experiments are restricted to a single DLM backbone (Dream-Coder-Instruct-7B) and a single domain (Python code generation); it is unclear whether the gains and conclusions transfer to general natural language generation or to other DLM architectures/vocabularies.

No experimental comparison against several closely related left-to-right coherence/verification baselines discussed at length in Related Work (e.g., APD, FlashDLLM, TiDAR, discrete copula diffusion), making it hard to assess CoDiLA's advantage over the broader literature rather than just ADJUST and the vanilla base model.

Results appear to be reported from single runs (n=1, fixed seed) without variance/confidence intervals, which weakens the statistical reliability of the reported Pareto-frontier improvements, especially on smaller benchmarks like HumanEval (164 problems).

The soft-conditioning interface relies on near-identical token ID spaces between the DLM (Dream-Coder) and AR (Qwen3) tokenizers, a convenient but somewhat fragile implementation detail that may not generalize to DLM/AR pairs with substantially different vocabularies, limiting the generality of the proposed interface.

The candidate-scoping heuristic (restricting unmasking to the nearest 10 blocks to avoid premature EOS) is an ad hoc engineering fix whose necessity undercuts the claimed benefit of retaining full bidirectional/non-causal flexibility of the DLM; this is acknowledged but left for future work.

Block size is only explored up to B=8 due to latency constraints, so it remains unclear how the accuracy/throughput trade-off and the theoretical benefit of larger blocks behave at larger scales or whether the AR component becomes a bottleneck.

The dynamic parallelism scheme's fallback logic (DLM confidence for k=1) and threshold-based block completion add some complexity/heuristics whose sensitivity and robustness are not deeply analyzed beyond a single sweep over threshold values on two benchmarks.

strengths: Well-motivated theoretical contribution: Theorem 3.2 formally quantifies the NELBO reduction from block-wise vs. token-wise conditional independence, extending prior related results (Huang et al. 2022; Liu et al. 2025a) to arbitrary block sizes with an explicit expression for the gap.

Theorem 3.3 (Frechet class restriction) provides a clean, non-trivial argument for why top-k truncated conditioning (used by prior AR-verifier baselines like APD/FlashDLLM) is theoretically insufficient to recover the true joint mode, directly motivating the paper's soft-conditioning design.

The proposed soft-conditioning interface (projecting DLM marginals into the AR embedding space via <think> boundary tokens) is a simple, cheap, and well-justified mechanism; ablations (Table 4, boundary-token NELBO comparison) support its necessity over top-k alternatives.

Strong empirical evidence that the small auxiliary AR model (0.6B) is not simply doing the coding task itself: standalone Qwen3-0.6B underperforms CoDiLA substantially, and scaling the AR model up (1.7B, 4B) gives no consistent gains, supporting the claim that it acts as a lightweight local coherence corrector rather than a strong generator.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across static parallelism, dynamic (threshold-based) parallelism, and a separate AR-verification mode, spanning multiple code benchmarks (HumanEval/+, MBPP/+, BigCodeBench full/hard) plus non-causal tasks (infilling, ParallelBench, graph traversal), demonstrating that CoDiLA establishes a new accuracy-throughput Pareto frontier and substantially reduces syntax-error rates (Table 1).

Careful attention to preserving DLM-specific capabilities: the Spearman correlation analysis (Appendix B.5) meaningfully demonstrates that CoDiLA retains more any-order/non-causal generation behavior than the vanilla DLM, addressing a key concern about left-to-right coherence-enforcement methods stripping away bidirectional advantages.

Extensive ablations (candidate scope, multi-block generation, batch-size throughput, AR model size) that probe the robustness and design choices of the method rather than reporting only headline numbers.
Detailed reproducibility information in the appendix (training data, hyperparameters, tokenizer alignment details, decoding algorithm specifics).
weaknesses: All main experiments are built on a single base DLM (Dream-Coder-Instruct-7B); it is unclear how well the soft-conditioning AR interface and the theoretical gains generalize to other DLM architectures, vocabularies, or non-code domains, limiting the demonstrated generality of the claimed 'new Pareto frontier'.

The empirical comparison to prior coherence-enforcement work is limited essentially to one baseline (ADJUST); other cited left-to-right/self-speculative methods (APD, FlashDLLM, TiDAR, discrete copula diffusion) are discussed but not empirically compared, making it harder to assess CoDiLA's relative advantage against the broader competitive landscape.

The three generation strategies (static parallelism, dynamic parallelism, AR-as-verifier) are evaluated on different subsets of tasks/benchmarks (verification mode only shown on ParallelBench/graph traversal, not on the main code benchmarks), so it's unclear how these modes compare directly to each other or whether the verifier mode would also improve standard code-gen accuracy/throughput.

Latency results emphasize batch size 1; while an appendix ablation shows overhead is amortized by batch size 8, this analysis is limited to a single configuration/benchmark, leaving open questions about how the method behaves under more realistic serving conditions (varying batch sizes, sequence lengths, concurrent requests).

The AR model is finetuned on the same SFT dataset used to train the base DLM, which, combined with the block-masking training procedure, raises a (not fully addressed) question of how much of the coherence gain stems from the AR learning dataset-specific n-gram/local patterns versus a more general coherence-modeling capability that would transfer to out-of-distribution code styles.

The theoretical contribution, while a valid and useful extension, is incremental relative to acknowledged prior work (Huang et al. 2022; Liu et al. 2025a; Kang et al. 2026; Zhong et al. 2026), and the core practical innovation (soft-conditioning via embedding expectation) is a relatively straightforward engineering idea, so the paper's novelty rests more on integration and thorough empirical validation than on a fundamentally new mechanism.

Block size is restricted to B<=8 in the main throughput-accuracy experiments due to the AR component's sequential cost, meaning the theoretically motivated benefit of arbitrarily large blocks (Theorem 3.2) is not actually realized in the practical latency-accuracy trade-off shown in the main results.

strengths: Clear theoretical motivation: Theorem 3.2 formally quantifies how block-wise factorization strictly reduces the irreducible NELBO relative to token-wise factorization, and Theorem 3.3 gives a principled argument (Fréchet class / copula argument) for why full soft-marginal conditioning is necessary rather than top-k truncation, motivating the design choice of soft-conditioning over simpler alternatives used in prior work (e.g., Hu et al., 2026; Israel et al., 2025).

The soft-conditioning interface (projecting DLM marginals into the AR embedding space, bracketed by <think>/<\think> tokens) is a simple, cheap, and reasonably novel way to couple a frozen large DLM with a small AR model without expensive full-sequence attention, unlike competing approaches (ADJUST, APD, TiDAR) that incur either higher overhead or loss of bidirectional/non-causal capability.

Reasonably thorough empirical evaluation: static and dynamic parallelism results across six code benchmarks, a direct head-to-head against a genuine competitor (ADJUST), a syntax-error-rate analysis isolating the source of gains, and multiple non-causal capability checks (HumanEval-Infilling, ParallelBench, graph traversal) that test whether bidirectionality is preserved.

Extensive ablations (soft vs. top-k conditioning, AR model size, candidate scope, multi-block generation, generation-order analysis, batch-size scaling) that probe the mechanism of the method rather than just reporting headline numbers, and that control for the possibility that gains simply come from the auxiliary AR model's own standalone coding ability (Qwen3-0.6B solo baseline).
Good reproducibility effort: detailed appendix on training protocol, tokenizer alignment, decoding hyperparameters, and hardware, which would facilitate replication.
weaknesses: All main results rely on a single DLM backbone (Dream-Coder-Instruct-7B) and a single AR family (Qwen3), run on a single GPU at a single model scale; the claim of 'establishing a new Pareto frontier' is therefore only demonstrated in one specific setting and generalization to other DLM backbones, scales, or AR families is untested.

The baseline Dream-Coder comparison uses naive fixed top-K unmasking rather than stronger existing entropy/threshold-based accelerated-decoding baselines from the literature (e.g., Fast-dLLM, dInfer, D2F, block-diffusion variants) that are discussed in Related Work but not empirically compared against in the main Pareto-frontier plots, making the 'new Pareto frontier' claim somewhat narrower than advertised.

Although the paper tries to rule out that gains stem from the AR model's own coding capability (via the standalone Qwen3-0.6B baseline), the AR model is still finetuned end-to-end on the same SFT corpus used for the DLM; it remains plausible that part of the improvement reflects the AR component effectively acting as a second, differently-biased generator/corrector rather than purely 'retrieving' DLM-consistent coherent completions, and this is not fully disentangled.

Reported accuracy numbers (Pass@1 on HumanEval/MBPP, ParallelBench, graph traversal) appear to be single-seed/single-sample (n=1) without variance estimates or multiple runs; some reported gains (e.g., graph traversal improvements of <1pp, ParallelBench K=2 where CoDiLA is actually slightly worse than baseline) are small enough that statistical significance is unclear, especially on small benchmarks like HumanEval (164 problems).

The practical benefit is capped by sequential AR cost within blocks: the paper itself restricts main experiments to B≤8 despite theory favoring larger blocks, so the realized latency gains are modest and the dynamic-parallelism results show that matching baseline accuracy requires giving up much of the speedup (back to roughly 2x), which is a fairly modest efficiency improvement for the additional system complexity (training a separate AR model per block size, dual-model serving).

Theorem 3.3's 'sufficiency' result is essentially a generic universal-approximation argument and does not specifically justify the chosen soft-conditioning mechanism (expectation of embeddings under the marginal) over other possible rich conditioning schemes; the connection between the abstract theorem and the concrete architectural choice is more heuristic than the paper's framing suggests.

The method requires training a separate AR model per block size (32k steps each) and maintaining two models concurrently in memory during inference, which adds non-trivial engineering/resource overhead that is somewhat underemphasized relative to the throughput gains reported.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: identifies conditional token independence bias in DLMs as the source of local incoherence in parallel decoding, with intuitive empirical illustration (Figure 1).

Solid theoretical contribution: Theorem 3.2 generalizes prior NELBO factorization analysis to block sizes B>1, formally proving that block-wise joint modeling strictly reduces irreducible loss; Theorem 3.3 gives a clean counterexample showing why top-k truncated marginals (used in competing methods) can provably exclude the true joint mode, well-motivating the soft-conditioning design.

Practical and lightweight architecture: the soft-conditioning interface (projecting DLM marginals into the AR embedding space) avoids expensive full-sequence AR verification and allows reuse of a small pretrained AR model with minimal additional training, addressing a real efficiency bottleneck in prior approaches like ADJUST and APD/FlashDLLM.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: results span static parallelism, dynamic (threshold) parallelism, and AR-based verification across multiple code benchmarks (HumanEval(+), MBPP(+), BigCodeBench), plus bidirectional/non-causal tasks (code infilling, ParallelBench, graph traversal), directly testing the central claim that CoDiLA preserves DLM-specific capabilities.

Strong and informative ablation suite: soft- vs top-k-conditioning, AR model scaling (showing small AR suffices), candidate scope/horizon, single vs multi-block generation, and Spearman-correlation analysis of generation order to verify any-order behavior is preserved — these ablations meaningfully substantiate the paper's design choices rather than just reporting headline numbers.
Transparent and detailed reproducibility documentation (Appendix A), including exact training/decoding hyperparameters, tokenizer alignment details, and evaluation protocol fixes.
weaknesses: Experiments are built on a single DLM backbone (Dream-Coder-Instruct-7B) and a single family of auxiliary AR models (Qwen3), restricting evidence that the method generalizes across different DLM architectures/scales or AR model families beyond the ablation on AR size.

Evaluation is concentrated almost entirely on code generation; while this is a reasonable focus given DLM scaling trends, the generality of the coherence benefits for broader natural language generation tasks is not empirically tested.

Baselines for coherence enforcement are somewhat limited: only ADJUST is directly compared in the main results, while other discussed related methods (APD/FlashDLLM, TiDAR, discrete copula diffusion) are not empirically benchmarked despite being closely related competitors.

Several design choices (local candidate scope of 10 blocks, EOS penalty, entropy mixture weight λ=0.5 for infilling, verification penalty of 1.0) appear to be manually tuned/heuristic without a principled selection procedure or sensitivity analysis beyond a few spot ablations.
A separate AR model must be trained per block size B, which increases deployment/training overhead and complicates practical adoption compared to a single flexible model.

Results appear to be reported from single runs (n=1) without variance across seeds or multiple samples, making it harder to assess the statistical robustness of reported Pass@1 differences, especially on smaller benchmarks like HumanEval (164 problems).
